title: An AI-driven DCC fan-game using Jev to classify each player input to ensure both flexibility and consistency
author: MathiasBack
selftext:
I’ve been building an open text-RPG based on Dungeon Crawler Carl as a hobby project for a couple of months. Most of the work ended up being architecture to stop the narration agent from inventing, hallucinating or gaslighting the player, so that’s what this post is mostly about. Maybe some of my learnings can be useful for others! 

My first version was the naïve one big prompt that did everything: picked the relevant player stat, rolled the dice, set the difficulty, wrote the scene and updated about 30 fields of state. It was basically grading its own exams, and it wanted the player to succeed. Measuring \~1000 turns across several rounds of rewriting the prompt, the player succeeded at whatever they tried to do 97.2% of the time. 

This meant you could basically write whatever you wanted and the game would find a way to make it work. It was fun and flexible, but also very easy as typing "I find the boss' weakness, attack it continually and avoid all its attacks" would work even against the toughest bosses. Also, stats kept updating out of the blue, items got used twice, and NPCs changed their background halfway through a conversation. 

As most others making similar hobby games realize, the narration agent cannot be allowed to change game state itself. I still wanted the game to be fully open and flexible, as well as allowing for LLM creativity. The rule now is that the narration model can suggest things, but only the engine changes any state. The engine is plain TypeScript with seeded dice, so I can replay any turn from the database. Anything the narration model returns is treated as untrusted input: it gets clamped and validated, and rejections are logged so I can improve the system over time.

Roughly how a turn works (visualized in the diagram):

1. The player writes their line. 
2. A classifier (Jev from Typesafe) interprets the text for intent, with roughly 350 question definitions. Each turn only sends the ones that apply based on the current game state, about 50 on a typical turn, usually taking 70-230 ms. 
3. The engine resolves the action such as any dice rolls, character movement, time spent, who you meet, and any damage. Much of this is decided using Jev, while other parts are decided purely by rules in the game engine. Sometimes it stops and asks you first: before something irreversible, when you can succeed at a cost, or a fight starts it's not obvious you're going to win.
4. The narrator (primarily Gemma 4) writes the scene from a summary of what the engine concluded. It only writes prose. No JSON or numbers.
5. A continuity check compares the narration text with the engine’s records. If the narrator walks through a door that doesn’t exist or brings back a dead companion, that part is struck and rewritten. This still happens on about 7% of turns, and I'm working on reducing this further. A recorder model reads the final text and suggests state changes. 

Numbers from last week (based on 2,300 turns in production, much of it bots playtesting): 

* the first words show up after about 5 seconds,
* the whole turn takes around 14 seconds, usually much quicker than the time it takes to read the narration,
* and the total cost is currently under a cent per turn, about $0.008.

Other critical lessons: 

* Don’t let regex decide what something is. My worst bugs all came from word lists. A baseball bat was filed as jewellery because its description included “it rings when it lands”. A hammer became armour because of the words “car boot”. A bipod “for a rifle” gave the player twelve rounds of ammo. I kept patching it with more words until I moved all the “what is this?” questions over to the Jev classifier once that launched. Regex is now only a fallback.
* I started out using Sonnet 5 for narration, which made the game way too expensive. For a long period, I tried several different narration agents, and landed on Gemma 4 as the best trade-off between low cost, low latency and still high quality. For the game guide, chat feature and the TV show scenes I use Kimi K3 for flavor. 

The DCC parts were the most fun to build. I have spent a lot of time and effort making sure it works and feels canon. I have even implemented "bugs" that are later patched in the books, such as killing enemies by bringing them into your inventory. The game currently covers the surface, Floors 1 and 2, and the televised shows in between.

If you would like to try it out:

* you can play it for free: [dungeon-crawler.mathiasplayground.dev](https://dungeon-crawler.mathiasplayground.dev/?r=z2e9y3)
   * it's a web-app working well on both desktop and mobile
   * note that an account/email is needed
* 2-minute video to view how it looks: [youtu.be](https://youtu.be/kjFJelCgK1s)

This is an unofficial, non-commercial fan project. I would love for more people to try the game out, but may reduce the now generous play limits if too many sign up at once.

comments.author: Enthusiasm_Brave
comments.body:
Looks cool! I have a tool that is similar I built for fun, and you're right that you have to guard tail the narrator or it will just invent new things every turn. 

A DCC is basically a TT RPG session with absolutely no wrong way to solve a problem. It would be like a Game Master that had every possible situation ready to go, but all the threads eventually lead to the same ending of freedom or death. Meanwhile the subplots, maybe antagonist AI, are running parallel  plots in the background to run into and run by their own Game Master. 

I searched a bit for something like this when I thought about starting my tool. I assumed someone started this type of project as soon as AI became capable enough and was surprised no one really had.

I feel like, cost allowing, at least the AI announcements would add so much if they were spoken instead of text. That sudden sound, inability to ask it to repeat itself less it becomes irritated, etc would add a lot of immersion. 

I mean, leave out the foot fetish stuff, but otherwise... (No offense to those with hamster smooshing foot fetishes!)

replies.author: MathiasBack
replies.body: Thanks! Yeah, reining the narrator in was most of the work. Left alone it happily hands you a sword you never picked up. The read-aloud idea is really good, especially for the system AI announcements, since in the books those are basically a booming voice in everyone's head. I might try a TTS pass on just those lines and see how it feels!

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
The 97.2% success rate is such a good stat to share, because it shows exactly why a model shouldn't grade its own exams. Treating the narrator's output as untrusted input that gets clamped and validated is the right fix, and seeded dice so you can replay any turn is a great debugging habit.

Your step 3 (stopping to ask before something irreversible) is close to what I landed on in Hatched, a browser city where every resident is an AI. A free local rules brain runs everyday life, and big choices like taking out a loan come to the player as a plain yes or no instead of being decided in prose. Out of curiosity, on that 7% of turns that fail the continuity check, is it usually the narrator inventing new things, or contradicting things the engine already recorded?

replies.author: MathiasBack
replies.body: Mostly contradicting, it turns out. I went through the logs, and of about 330 first drafts that got struck, close to half were the narrator putting the player somewhere the engine says they aren't. After that come smaller buckets like wrong gear, dead monsters still standing, and things that happened earlier being retold wrong. Actually inventing stuff is rarer, mostly extra enemies that don't exist, and it shows up more in the fight summaries than in normal turns. Hatched looks interesting, by the way, I'll check it out.
